awd_titl_txt: Conference: Structure-Preserving Scientific Computing and Machine Learning Summer School and Hackathon
awd_abstract_narration:
A Summer School and Hackathon event on Structure-Preserving Scientific Computing and Machine Learning will take place at the University of Washington, Seattle on June 16-25, 2025. Structure-Preserving Scientific Computing is an emerging field of research focused on the design of efficient numerical methods or algorithms that preserve fundamental mathematical structures or properties of continuous models at the discrete level. Such approaches are often essential to maintain accuracy and stability of numerical solutions, as well as to enhance efficiency in large-scale simulations. Moreover, scientific machine learning, which utilizes machine learning techniques to solve scientific computing problems, can also benefit from incorporating structure-preserving ideas to improve their prediction capability and generalizability on data-driven models. The main objectives of this Summer School and Hackathon event are: 1) Create a synergistic opportunity for established researchers, industry partners, postdocs, and graduate students to meet, network, and share the latest cutting-edge research in structure-preserving scientific computing. 2) Engage and provide training to graduate students working in computational mathematics. 3) Enable early career researchers to form strong connections and receive mentorship with world-leading experts and industry project leaders. 4) Cultivate long-lasting collaborations and innovative research among students and researchers at all career stages from academia, government agencies, industry, and beyond. 

The Summer School will feature world-renowned experts delivering four minicourses on topics in Structure-Preserving Scientific Computing and Machine Learning, including operator splitting, dynamical low-rank methods, neural ordinary differential equations (ODEs), and neural operators. Building on this synergy, the subsequent Hackathon will challenge students to apply their newly acquired knowledge to real-world applications through four projects, led by project leaders from academia, government agencies, industry, and national laboratories. Event details and applications for graduate student participation will be posted on the conference website: https://sites.google.com/view/crg-spd/events/seattle-2025.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Structure-preserving scientific computing is an emerging area of research focused on the design of eﬃcient numerical methods that preserve fundamental mathematical structures or properties of continuous models at the discrete level. Such methods are essential for maintaining accuracy and stability of numerical solutions, as well as enhancing efficiency for large-scale simulations. Moreover, scientific machine learning techniques that incorporate structure-preserving principles can also be beneficial to enhance robustness, predictive accuracy, and generalizability.


Motivated by these recent developments, we organized a 10-day Summer School and Hackathon on Structure-Preserving Scientific Computing and Machine Learning, held from June 16 to 25, 2025, at the University of Washington in Seattle. The event was highly successful -- we welcomed 36 graduate students from 21 institutions across the United States and Canada, in addition to local participants at the University of Washington. 


The five-day Summer School featured four minicourses delivered by three world-leading experts: Chris Budd (University of Bath), Lukas Einkemmer (University of Innsbruck), and Raymond Spiteri (University of Saskatchewan). The minicourses covered a wide range of topics that intersects structure-preserving scientific computing and machine learning. Building on this foundation, the following three-day Hackathon engaged students in four collaborative projects led by experts from academia (Oliver J. Bear Don't Walk IV, University of Washington), government agency (Stephane Gaudreault, Environment Canada), industry (John Coughlin, Pasteur Labs & ISI), and national laboratory (Terry Haut, Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory). The event was further supported by several postdoctoral researchers and faculty members.


Overall, the Summer School and Hackathon fostered active engagements among graduate students, postdoctoral researchers, established academics, and practitioners from industry and government. Participants received advanced training in computational mathematics, exchanged ideas through lectures, discussions, and hands-on collaboration, and formed new professional connections. These interactions helped seed innovative research directions and established collaborations across career stages and different sectors, which are expected to continue well beyond this event.
